catalog_quote: アクセントは日本語と同じように高低アクセントである。しかし日本語のアクセントとは性格が違う。日本語では、どこまでが高く、どこからが低くなるかが重要なポイントであるが、アイヌ語では、どこまでが低く、どこから高くなるかがポイントである。語によって上昇するところがきまっており、それより前はすべて低く、それよりあとは抑揚（イントネーション）によって上がったりしなければ、だんだん低くなることが多い。 アクセントは地方によって違うが、沙流方言では、低から高へ上がる位置に関して著しい傾向がある。すなわち 第一音節が開音節ならば第二音節から高くなる。 sapá サパ 頭 ku=sápaha クサパハ 私の頭 第一音節が閉音節ならば第一音節が高い。 sínrit シンリッ 先祖 k=óyra コイラ 私は忘れた 表記上は、この傾向に合っているときは「´」をつけずにsapa, ku=sapaha, sinrit, k=oyraのように書き、この傾向に合わないとき（例外的なとき）のみ、アクセント記号を母音字の上につけて示す。 húci フチ おばあちゃん k=étuhu ケトゥフ 私の鼻 a=akíhi アアキヒ （引用文中で）私の弟 ecioká エチオカ あなたたち
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Hokkaido Ainu (ainu1240) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had one item, Shiraishi 2001 'Prosodic Structure and Sandhi Phenomena in the Saru Dialect of Ainu' (De Gruyter, doi:10.1515/9783110885989.141). The DOI is closed (Unpaywall/S2: CLOSED; De Gruyter returns an empty 202; not on HathiTrust or archive.org), but the author's SGU homepage links a self-archived 13-page preprint, which was downloaded and read (saved as under, updated). It is about consonant sandhi (n-/r-alternation) and the prosodic phrasing domains that govern it; it contains no statement about word accent/stress placement (accent/stress/pitch never occur in the text) -> prosody-but-not-word-stress, priority none. The best first-hand accent statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Tamura 1996 (Saru dialect dictionary appendix, ③アクセント, already held by the project from the earlier stage): pitch accent, rise on syllable 1 if the initial syllable is closed, on syllable 2 if it is open, lexical exceptions marked. Lead seen on the author's publication list but not downloaded (no PDF offered): Shiraishi 1998b 'Evidence for Prominence-based Accent Shifting in Ainu (the Saru Dialect)', Proc. 117th Meeting of the Linguistic Society of Japan, 266-271 — likely a direct word-accent source; medium priority to acquire.

new_statements.quote: アクセントは日本語と同じように高低アクセントである。しかし日本語のアクセントとは性格が違う。…アイヌ語では、どこまでが低く、どこから高くなるかがポイントである。語によって上昇するところがきまっており、それより前はすべて低く、それよりあとは抑揚（イントネーション）によって上がったりしなければ、だんだん低くなることが多い。アクセントは地方によって違うが、沙流方言では、低から高へ上がる位置に関して著しい傾向がある。すなわち 第一音節が開音節ならば第二音節から高くなる。sapá《頭》 ku=sápaha《私の頭》 第一音節が閉音節ならば第一音節が高い。sínrit《先祖》 k=óyra《私は忘れた》 表記上は、この傾向に合っているときは「´」をつけずにsapa, ku=sapaha, sinrit, k=oyraのように書き、この傾向に合わないとき（例外的なとき）のみ、アクセント記号を母音字の上につけて示す。húci《おばあちゃん》 k=étuhu《私の鼻》 a=akíhi《私の弟》 ecioká《あなたたち》
new_statements.translation: The accent is a high-low (pitch) accent, as in Japanese, but of a different character. ... In Ainu the point is up to where the pitch is low and from where it becomes high. The place of the rise is fixed for each word; everything before it is low, and after it, unless raised by intonation, the pitch mostly falls gradually. Accent differs by region, but in the Saru dialect there is a marked tendency in the position of the low-to-high rise, namely: if the first syllable is open, the pitch becomes high from the second syllable: sapá 'head', ku=sápaha 'my head'. If the first syllable is closed, the first syllable is high: sínrit 'ancestor', k=óyra 'I forgot'. In the notation, words that follow this tendency are written without the acute (sapa, ku=sapaha, sinrit, k=oyra); only when a word does not follow it (exceptional cases) is the accent mark written over the vowel: húci 'grandmother', k=étuhu 'my nose', a=akíhi 'my younger brother', ecioká 'you (pl.)'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each word has one low-to-high pitch rise (a pitch accent) whose position is predictable from the weight of the first syllable: if the first syllable is closed (CVC) the accent is on the first syllable; if it is open (CV) the accent is on the second syllable. Words that deviate from this are lexically marked exceptions (húci, k=étuhu, a=akíhi, ecioká; Itabashi cites tere, pase, teta with initial accent despite open first syllable). Hokkaido Ainu has no vowel-length contrast, so weight is closed vs open syllable only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress; Tamura describes one rise per word with gradual fall afterwards (post-accent syllables low/falling unless intonation raises them).
new_statements.exceptions: Yes: the rule is called a 'marked tendency' (著しい傾向), not exceptionless; exceptional words are marked with an acute in the dictionary (húci 'grandmother', k=étuhu 'my nose', a=akíhi 'my younger brother', ecioká 'you (pl.)'); the NINJAL topical dictionary adds rúra 'to carry'. Accent varies regionally; Itabashi 2001 (citing Hattori 1964) reports that the Bihoro, Samani and Kushiro (Haruyama) dialects lack a phonemic pitch contrast (one-pattern accent).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: the domain is the phonological word including person prefixes (ku=sápaha, k=óyra: the prefix counts as first syllable, so k=óyra 'I forgot' has the accent on the first syllable of the word oyra.. i.e. the closed syllable koy-), as shown by the examples. Realization is pitch (高低アクセント), not intensity; the source explicitly contrasts it with Japanese. Dictionary citation forms; sentence intonation is treated separately (④イントネーション). Describes the Saru dialect (Southern Hokkaido); the NINJAL sites (Nakagawa/Bugaeva) generalize the same rule to Ainu as documented in their Saru/Chitose corpora.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement describes the Saru (沙流) dialect of Southern Hokkaido Ainu (Tamura's speakers from the Saru river valley, Biratori area), which Glottolog subsumes under Hokkaido Ainu (ainu1240); a dialect-level glottocode was not verified. Tamura states that accent differs regionally, and Itabashi 2001 (after Hattori 1964) reports Bihoro, Samani and Kushiro (Haruyama) dialects without a phonemic pitch contrast, so the rule should be filed as Saru/Southern Hokkaido Ainu rather than all of ainu1240. The NINJAL corpus sites (Saru and Chitose dialects) restate the same rule.

new_statements.translation: The accent is a pitch accent, as in Japanese, but of a different character. [...] In Ainu the point is how far the word stays low and where it rises. Each word has a fixed place where it rises; everything before it is low. [...] In the Saru dialect there is a marked tendency regarding where the rise from low to high falls: if the first syllable is open, the word becomes high from the second syllable (sapá 'head', ku=sápaha 'my head'); if the first syllable is closed, the first syllable is high (sínrit 'ancestor', k=óyra 'I forgot'). [...] Only when a word does not fit this tendency (exceptions) is the accent mark written on the vowel: húci 'grandmother', k=étuhu 'my nose', a=akíhi 'my younger brother', ecioká 'you (pl.)'.
new_statements.citation: Tamura Suzuko 田村すず子 (1996). アイヌ語沙流方言辞典 [Ainu Saru-dialect dictionary]. Tokyo: Sōfūkan. Appendix 「アイヌ語沙流方言略説」, §1 音韻, ③アクセント (reproduced verbatim on the National Ainu Museum Ainu Language Archive).
new_statements.locator: Appendix 「アイヌ語沙流方言略説」 §1 音韻 ③アクセント (printed appendix pp. 1-19 of Tamura 1996; web reproduction, section ③)
new_statements.reading: Hokkaido (Saru) Ainu has a lexical pitch accent (low-then-high rise) whose default placement is weight-sensitive at the left edge: closed initial syllable -> accent on syllable 1; open initial syllable -> accent on syllable 2; lexical exceptions exist and are marked. This is a first-hand statement by the dialect's principal descriptive linguist. The single works with stress in the title (Shiraishi 2001) adds nothing on accent placement.

sources.note: High-low (pitch) accent; the low-to-high rise is on the 2nd syllable if the 1st syllable is open (sapá, ku=sápaha), on the 1st syllable if it is closed (sínrit, k=óyra); exceptions marked with acute (húci, k=étuhu, a=akíhi, ecioká); a 'marked tendency' of the Saru dialect, accent differs by region.

sources.note: 'Here [Yezo Ainu] the tonic accent is quite unimportant and many would hardly notice it. The principal thing is to clearly define every syllable and pronounce it distinctly' — contrasts with Saghalien 'tones'; older, impressionistic, superseded.

sources.citation: Shiraishi, Hidetoshi (2001). Prosodic Structure and Sandhi Phenomena in the Saru Dialect of Ainu. In Jeroen van de Weijer & Tetsuo Nishihara (eds), Issues in Japanese Phonology and Morphology, 141-158. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
sources.quote: This paper examines the consonantal sandhi phenomena of Ainu and points out that a similar distinction can be observed in at least two sandhi processes centering on n and r, which we will term n-alternation and r-alternation, respectively. [...] An examination of a corpus of the Saru dialect reveals that the n-alternation is sensitive to a certain syntactic boundary (and hence a P-structure rule), but the r-alternation is not (and hence is a Pure phonological rule).
sources.locator: §1 Introduction p. 1 and §4 Conclusion p. 12 of the author copy (= pp. 141-142, 157 of the printed chapter)
sources.note: Nothing. The chapter is about consonant sandhi (n- and r-alternation, e.g. pon yuk > po[y] yuk, an wa > a[m m]a) and the prosodic phrasing domains that govern it (sentence boundary blocks n-alternation; r-alternation applies across it). The words accent/stress/pitch do not occur in the text; no statement of where word accent falls. It cites Shiraishi (1998) M.A. thesis on consonant sandhi only.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Ainu language' (raw wikitext, 2026-09-17)
sources.note: 'The Ainu language also has a pitch accent system. Generally, words containing affixes have a high pitch on a syllable in the stem. This will typically fall on the first syllable if that is long (has a final consonant or a diphthong), and will otherwise fall on the second syllable, though there are exceptions.' Tertiary; used only as a pointer.

sources.citation: Nakagawa Hiroshi, Anna Bugaeva, Mika Fukazawa & Miki Kobayashi (eds). 2016-2021. A Glossed Audio Corpus of Ainu Folklore. Tokyo: NINJAL (website, 'Notes on transcription')
sources.note: 'The Ainu language has a high-low accent.. Typically, the accent comes to the second syllable if the first syllable is an open syllable, and to the first syllable if the first syllable is a closed syllable. However, there are some exceptions, so refer to Tamura (1996) to check the accent for each word.'

sources.citation: Bugaeva, Anna & Shiho Endō (eds). 2015-. A Topical Dictionary of Conversational Ainu (Saru dialect, speaker Setsu Kurokawa). Tokyo: NINJAL (website, notes on transcription)
sources.note: 'Typically, the accent in the Ainu language comes to the second syllable if the first syllable is an open syllable, and to the first syllable if the first syllable is a closed syllable. Accent marks are not indicated for words that follow this rule. There are some words to which this rule does not apply (e.g. rúra to carry).'

sources.note: §1a 5) (pp. 88-89, examples from Hattori 1964): pitch accent is phonemic in Hokkaido Ainu, the low-to-high rise is distinctive; in most dialects the accent kernel is on the 2nd syllable if the 1st is open (sapa LH, sapaha LHL, kusapaha LHLL; exceptions tere HL, pase HL, teta HL) and on the 1st if it is closed (sikup HL, penram HL, itotkir HL); Bihoro, Samani and Kushiro (Haruyama) dialects have no phonemic pitch contrast (one-pattern accent). Second-hand comparative summary.
